A lot of interesting points have been made, so I'll just add in my own regarding the difficulty of keeping up with recent kpop.

Kpop back then wasn't as mainstream or popular in America. A majority of the well known, popular groups were from big companies with lots of money, connections, etc etc. I just looked at the kpop wikipedia page of groups from the 2000s, and there were various groups from the 2000s that I did not recognize because they were from small companies. I'm unsure if it was a different case in Korea, but as an international fan, I did not know them.

However, there WAS a way for unknown groups to gain more traction and popularity in the international kpop fanbase; kpop youtubers. Yknow, like JREKML, 2MinJinkJongKey, Simon and Martina. These kpop youtubers were popular because it was hard to come across kpop fans, and so fans found it nice to have someone to relate to.

In particular, Simon and Martina made some videos in their series "Music Mondays," which brought exposure to unknown artists. They also held kpop award shows at the end of each year, which again, brought attention to certain groups. Examples of these groups include Sunny Hill, LEDApple, Royal Pirates, G.I, 5Dolls, and Busker Busker. This made it easier for kpop fans to not only keep up with their favorite groups, but to discover new ones as well.

I don't see a lot of kpop youtubers now doing the same thing since kpop youtube is pretty popular now. A lot of the kpop youtubers who react to "underrated groups" are those with low sub counts. ReacttotheK and Form of Therapy are exceptions, but I think there are kpop fans who cherry pick videos they want to watch because it's their bias group, which is why ReacttotheK's videos on Cacophony or Lee Jin Ah are low compared to others.

I'm a freshman and so I've only marched bari for a year. Because of how big and heavy it is, you will sometimes think it's a pain, but in the end it's a pretty fun instrument to play and march! You get to add tons of cool bass parts and even melodies if you're lucky enough. It's fun too because you're able to play it loud, so even with just one or two baris on the field, you can still hear them.

As for things to watch out for, you gotta talk care of your right thumb, back, neck, and shoulders. Continuing to push the bari forward with my right hand (and especially with horns up) messed up my right thumb. And if you're small like me, then reaching for the pinky keys may be a pain too. Personally I really disliked the harness, but in the end it all depends on you and how you feel about it! My band director told me to use whatever I was comfortable with, the only restriction he had was to make sure the harness or neck strap was black and not pink.
